about.title: Sikhism
about.length_note: About 25 minutes. The class covers seven topics, including the ten Gurus. Each idea gets one short step and, usually, a check question. Pause after any check question if you want more time.

say.text: Welcome to class five. Today we learn about Sikhism, a faith that began in the Punjab region of South Asia over five hundred years ago.

show.text: Sikhism

say.text: We will meet the Gurus, the core beliefs, the holy book, the gurdwara and its free kitchen, the Khalsa, a festival, and where Sikhs live. We describe it as Sikhs describe it.

show.text:
1. The Gurus
2. Core beliefs
3. The Guru Granth Sahib
4. The gurdwara and langar
5. The Khalsa and the Five Ks
6. Vaisakhi
7. Where Sikhs live

say.text: First, a key word. Sikhs explain the word Guru as meaning remover of darkness.

show.text: Guru = remover of darkness

say.text: The first Guru was Guru Nanak. He was born in 1469 in Talvandi, now called Nankana Sahib, in present-day Pakistan.

show.text: A 19th-century mural painting of Guru Nanak, from a gurdwara in Punjab

say.text: Sikh sources say that at about age thirty, Guru Nanak had a profound mystical revelation. Sikhs honour him as the founder of their faith.

show.text: Founder: Guru Nanak (1469-1539)

ask.why: Sikhism was established by Guru Nanak (1469-1539) and then led by nine other Gurus.

say.text: After Guru Nanak came nine more Gurus. In all there were ten human Gurus, from 1469 to 1708.

show.text: Ten human Gurus

say.text: Sikhs believe all ten Gurus carried the same spirit. Their styles differed because their times differed.

show.text: One spirit, ten Gurus

ask.q: How many human Gurus did Sikhism have?
ask.why: There were ten human Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh.

say.text: Here they are in order. You do not need to memorise them. Just notice the first, Nanak, and the last, Gobind Singh.

show.text:
1 Nanak
2 Angad
3 Amar Das
4 Ram Das
5 Arjan
6 Hargobind
7 Har Rai
8 Har Krishan
9 Tegh Bahadur
10 Gobind Singh

say.text: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, finished the Golden Temple at Amritsar. He built it with a door on each of its four sides.

show.text: Four doors: a welcome for all

say.text: The doors stand for a welcome to people of every faith and background. That idea of welcome will come back when we reach the kitchen.

show.text: The Golden Temple (Sri Harmandir Sahib) in Amritsar, with its pool and gold-covered shrine

say.text: Sikh history also includes hard times. Guru Arjan is remembered as the first Sikh martyr. He was executed by the Mughal ruler Jahangir in 1606. Sikh tradition says it was for refusing to remove parts of the Adi Granth; Jahangir's own memoir links it to the Guru's support for a rebel prince.

show.text: Guru Arjan: first Sikh martyr (died 1606)

say.text: The ninth Guru, Tegh Bahadur, is remembered as the second Sikh martyr. He was executed in 1675 for defending Hindu Brahmins from forced conversion.

show.text: Guru Tegh Bahadur: second Sikh martyr (died 1675)

ask.q: Which Guru is remembered as the first Sikh martyr?
ask.why: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, is considered the first Sikh martyr.

say.text: Now the beliefs. The first is that there is one God. The Sikh scripture opens with the words Ik Onkar, which mean One God.

show.text: Ik Onkar: there is one God

say.text: Sikhs often call God Waheguru, meaning wonderful God. They say the one God is the Lord of all religions, and Sikhs do not claim exclusive rights to God.

show.text: Waheguru = 'wonderful God'

ask.why: Ik Onkar opens the Sikh scripture and speaks of God's oneness.

say.text: The second belief is equality. Sikh teaching holds that all people are equal before God. The Gurus also stressed the full equality of women.

show.text: Equality of all people

say.text: Here is a line attributed to Guru Nanak. It links belief to daily life.

show.text: "Truth is the highest virtue, but higher still is truthful living." (Guru Nanak, as quoted)

say.text: The third idea is service. Guru Nanak gave Sikhs three guidelines, often called the three pillars. Each one tells you what to do.

show.text:
Naam Japna: remember God
Kirat Karni: earn an honest living
Vand Chakna: share with others

say.text: Naam japna means meditating on God, by reciting, chanting or singing. Kirat karni means honest work. Vand chakna means sharing what you have with the community.

show.text:
Inside: remember God (naam japna)
Outside: honest work (kirat karni) and sharing (vand chakna)

ask.q: Which pillar means earning an honest living?
ask.why: Kirat karni is honest living. Naam japna is remembering God, and vand chakna is sharing.

say.text: Next, the holy book. The Guru Granth Sahib is also called the Adi Granth. Sikhs treat it as their living, eternal Guru.

show.text: One book, treated as a living Guru

say.text: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, declared that the scripture would be the Guru after him. That ended the line of human Gurus.

show.text: Guru Gobind Singh: the Granth is the eternal Guru (1708)

ask.q: Who declared the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru?
ask.why: The tenth Guru declared that the scripture would be the eternal Guru. Guru Arjan compiled the first edition, the Adi Granth.

say.text: What is inside? Compositions by six of the Gurus, and hymns by saints from other traditions. It runs to about 1430 pages.

show.text:
Writings of six Gurus
Hymns of saints from other traditions
About 1430 pages

say.text: The whole book is written as poetry and music. So most of a Sikh worship service is sung.

show.text: Scripture as poetry and song

say.text: Because it is the Guru, the book is treated like royalty. It sits on a raised platform under a canopy, and a whisk called a chaur is waved over it.

show.text: The Guru Granth Sahib on a raised platform under a canopy, with a chaur whisk waved above it

say.text: That brings us to the gurdwara, the Sikh place of learning and worship. The Guru Granth Sahib sits at its centre.

show.text: Gurdwara: place of learning and worship

say.text: Sikhism has no ordained clergy. Any woman or man from the congregation may lead worship.

show.text: No ordained clergy

say.text: Visitors take off their shoes and cover their heads as signs of respect. Everyone sits on the floor together. Visitors do not have to bow.

show.text:
Shoes off
Head covered
Sit on the floor, all together
Bowing is not required of visitors

ask.q: What do visitors do on entering a gurdwara?
ask.right: Remove their shoes and cover their heads
wrong: Stay silent for the whole service
ask.why: Shoes off and heads covered are signs of respect. There is no fee, and worship is mostly sung.

say.text: Now the langar, the gurdwara's community kitchen. It serves meals free to all, whatever their religion, caste, gender, wealth or ethnicity.

show.text: Langar: the free community kitchen

say.text: People sit on the floor and eat together as equals. The meals are vegetarian, so that no one is shut out of the table.

show.text: Rows of people of all ages sitting on the floor in a langar hall, sharing a simple meal

say.text: Volunteers run the kitchen. This is called seva, selfless service. Sikhs say langar is not charity but a spiritual practice and a way to build community.

show.text: Seva = selfless service

say.text: Sikh tradition says Guru Nanak started the practice, and Guru Angad is remembered for making it standard in every gurdwara. At big gurdwaras, teams cook for thousands of guests each day.

show.text:
Guru Nanak: begins the community kitchen
Guru Angad: makes it a standard part of every gurdwara
Today: nearly every gurdwara has a langar

ask.q: Who is welcome to eat at a langar?
ask.right: Everyone, whatever their religion, caste, gender or wealth
ask.why: Langar serves meals free of charge to all, with no distinction of religion, caste, gender or wealth.

say.text: Now the Khalsa. In 1699, at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh asked for volunteers willing to give their lives for the faith. Five stepped forward.

show.text: The five volunteers

say.text: They were initiated first and called the Panj Pyare, the Five Beloved Ones. They formed the core of the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs.

show.text: Panj Pyare = the Five Beloved Ones

say.text: Khalsa Sikhs wear five articles of faith, called the Five Ks because each name begins with the same K sound in Punjabi. Here they are.

show.text:
Kesh: uncut hair
Kara: steel bracelet
Kangha: comb
Kirpan: sword
Kachchera: undergarment

say.text: Not every Sikh has taken initiation. A Sikh who follows the Guru Granth Sahib but has not been initiated is called a Sahajdhari Sikh.

show.text:
Amritdhari (Khalsa): initiated, keeps the Five Ks
Sahajdhari: follows the Guru Granth Sahib, not initiated

ask.q: Which of the Five Ks is the steel bracelet?
ask.why: Kara is the steel bracelet. Kangha is the comb, kirpan the sword, and kesh uncut hair.

say.text: The Khalsa was founded on Vaisakhi. This is a major Sikh festival, and also a harvest festival in Punjab.

show.text: Vaisakhi: birth of the Khalsa, and a Punjab harvest festival

say.text: Khalsa Sikhs celebrate the order's birth on April 13 or 14 each year. Sikhs also keep gurpurabs, festivals for the Gurus. Guru Nanak's birthday falls on the November full moon.

show.text:
Vaisakhi: April 13 or 14
Guru Nanak's birthday: November full moon
Gurpurabs often include a 48-hour reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib

ask.q: What does Vaisakhi commemorate for Sikhs?
ask.right: The founding of the Khalsa in 1699
wrong: The death of Guru Gobind Singh
The writing of the Guru Granth Sahib
ask.why: Vaisakhi marks the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa. Guru Nanak's birthday is a separate festival.

say.text: Last topic: where Sikhs live today. Sikhism began in Punjab, and most Sikhs still live in India.

show.text: South Asia, with Punjab marked, then dots for Canada, the UK, the US, Australia, Italy and Malaysia

say.text: The 2011 Indian census counted about 20.8 million Sikhs, or 1.7 percent of India's people. Estimates for the world run from about 25 to 30 million.

show.text: 25-30 million Sikhs worldwide (estimate)

say.text: Pew counts Sikhs inside a group called other religions. That whole group is about two percent of the world's people.

show.text: Pew's 'other religions': about 2.2% of the world

say.text: This pie shows one estimate. India holds nearly nine in ten Sikhs. Different counts give somewhat different shares.

show.text: Share of the world's Sikhs

say.text: Outside India, the biggest Sikh communities are in Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, Italy and Malaysia. In Canada, Sikhs are about 2 percent of the population.

show.text: Sikh population outside India (census or estimate years differ)

ask.q: Which country has the most Sikhs?
ask.why: India has by far the most, about 20.8 million in the 2011 census and an estimated 23.8 million by 2023.

say.text: Sikhs have lived in the United States for more than 130 years. Many Sikh communities around the world are made of families who moved from Punjab.

show.text: A worldwide community

say.text: Let's put it together. One God. Equality. Service. Ten Gurus. A living Guru in a book. A kitchen open to all.

show.text:
One God (Ik Onkar)
Equality and service
Ten human Gurus, then the Guru Granth Sahib
Gurdwara and langar
Khalsa, Five Ks and Vaisakhi
Mostly in India, with communities worldwide

ask.right: Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib as their living, eternal Guru.
wrong: Langar is only for Sikh men.
Sikhs have had only one Guru.
ask.why: After the ten human Gurus, Sikhs regard the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru. Langar is for everyone.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, a voyage that opened the way for European colonization of the Americas.
Martin Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses in Wittenberg, Germany, which is often seen as the start of the Protestant Reformation.
Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in northern India, founding the Mughal dynasty. Later Gurus lived under Mughal rule.

other_side.claim: Guru Nanak received a revelation and founded a new religion.
other_side.other_view: Sikh sources describe a profound revelation to Guru Nanak and a distinct faith. Some outside summaries describe Sikhism as combining aspects of Hinduism and Islam, and note that Nanak grew up in a Hindu family in a village of both Hindus and Muslims. Sikhs generally do not describe their faith as a blend.

Sikh sources credit Guru Nanak with establishing the community kitchen. Others credit Guru Angad, the second Guru, with systematising it in gurdwaras, and one source names him as its creator. Both views agree it began with the early Gurus.

other_side.claim: The Khalsa was founded on Vaisakhi in 1699, and the date is settled.
other_side.other_view: Britannica gives March 30, 1699, according to some records, while Khalsa Sikhs celebrate it on April 13 or 14. Scholars also note that the word Khalsa was used before 1699, so how the order took shape is discussed in detail.

other_side.claim: About 90 percent of the world's Sikhs live in India, and there are about 25-30 million Sikhs.
other_side.other_view: Counts differ. One estimate gives India 89.75% of Sikhs, while another gives 83-84%. For the United States, Pew estimated about 200,000 Sikhs in 2012, while Sikh organisations cite figures up to 1,000,000 without sources. Many national censuses do not ask about religion.
